title: Dual-mode temperature sensor based on ferroelectric Bi0.5Na0.5TiO3 materials for robotic tactile perception
abstract: Temperature perception can allow robots to acquire rich information regarding their surroundings to improve the accuracy of both object manipulation and object recognition. However, existing robotic temperature perception systems mainly depend on thermoresistive effect, suffering from singular functionality and high energy consumption. Here, we demonstrate a ferroelectric Bi 0.5 Na 0.5 TiO 3 -based dual-mode temperature sensor for robotic temperature perception. The dual-mode temperature sensor can operate in a passive mode to perceive temperature variations by generating pyroelectric signals, and work in an active mode to detect static temperatures by producing pyro-photoelectric signals. Equipped with the dual-mode temperature sensor, a robot hand can perceive multi-dimensional temperature information and assess the thermal conductivity of materials, allowing identification of different materials in real-time with a high accuracy of 97.2 %. By combining passive and active temperature perception, the proposed dual-mode temperature sensor therefore holds significant potential for future robotic perception and manipulation.

title: High-bandwidth self-powered vibration sensors based on triboelectric particle-surface interactions
abstract: Vibrating triboelectric nanogenerators have the potential as self-powered vibration sensors if they can be designed to operate over a wide frequency band. Herein, we present a high-bandwidth self-powered triboelectric particle-surface vibration sensor. The sensor consists of a flat round capsule, filling with dielectric particles. The inner surfaces of the capsule are made of triboelectric materials backed by electrodes. When attached to a vibrating structure, the impact of the particles on the inner surfaces of the capsule causes them to be oppositely charged, and the dynamic motion of the charged particles in turn generates an alternating voltage across the two electrodes. A systematic investigation of the effects of particle properties, including material type, diameter, and packing ratio on the sensor’s output performance revealed that, among several designs, the combination of nylon particles and PTFE triboelectric layers yielded the highest output performance. The sensor’s flat frequency response has been found to span between 500 Hz and 7000 Hz, which is significantly higher than the recently reported values for triboelectric vibration sensors. Furthermore, the novel vibration sensor offers a frequency resolution of 0.19% at frequencies up to 8 kHz. The potentials of this new type of vibration sensor have been demonstrated for speech recognition applications and to detect structural vibrations due to drop-weight impact at different distances and heights.

title: Textile beeswax triboelectric nanogenerator as self-powered sound detectors and mechano-acoustic energy harvesters
abstract: The development of self-powered sensing technologies embedded in textiles is a cornerstone for enabling radically novel healthcare, well-being and defence solutions. The steppingstone for these advances is a new class of unconventional energy harvesters able to convert presently unused sources from our living environment such as sounds and vibrations into electrical energy. These generators would have to be flexible, mechanically robust, lightweight, resilient and they should produce a viable electric output. Here we present a novel textile-integrated triboelectric nanogenerator capable of sensing and harvesting low-frequency acoustic energy. These capabilities are enabled by a unique combination of materials such as beeswax as a triboelectric layer and graphene-based electrode, endowing multiple functionalities. Specifically, our device can sense ground-borne sounds in the 10-200 Hz frequency range, detect human voices, recognise human emotions, and harvest energy from environmental noise and vibrations. Additionally, the dynamic molecular interactions and the hydrophobic nature of the triboelectric layer provide intrinsic self-healing, water-repellent, and self-cleaning features, ensuring device functionality in bending and humidity environments.
